content: In October 2009, ACIP approved the 2010 Adult Immunization Schedule, which included several updates and changes. A bivalent human papillomavirus vaccine (HPV2) was licensed for use in females in October 2009. ACIP recommends that females receive either HPV2 or the quadrivalent human papillomavirus vaccine (HPV4). Additionally, HPV4 was licensed for use in males in October 2009, and ACIP issued a permissive recommendation for its use in males. Introductory statements were added to the footnotes for vaccines against measles, mumps, rubella, influenza, pneumococcal disease, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and meningococcal disease. Clarifications were made to the footnotes for vaccines against measles, mumps, rubella, influenza, hepatitis A, meningococcal disease, and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Specific schedule information was added to the hepatitis B vaccine footnote. The meningococcal vaccine footnote (11) now specifies which vaccine formulations are preferred for adults aged ≤55 years and ≥56 years, as well as which formulations are appropriate for revaccination. New examples were added to clarify who should and should not be considered for revaccination. The Hib vaccine footnote (13) was updated to specify which high-risk individuals may receive a single dose of the Hib vaccine. The Recommended Adult Immunization Schedule has been endorsed by ACIP, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the American College of Physicians. Adults with an uncertain or incomplete history of the primary vaccination series for tetanus and diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines should begin or complete the primary series. This series consists of three doses: the first two doses should be administered at least four weeks apart, and the third dose should be given 6–12 months after the second dose. Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis) can substitute for any one of the doses in the three-dose primary series. A booster dose of a tetanus and diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine should be administered to adults who have completed the primary series if the last dose was received ≥10 years ago. Either Tdap or Td (tetanus and diphtheria) vaccine may be used, as appropriate. For pregnant women, if the last Td vaccination was received ≥10 years ago, Td should be administered during the second or third trimester. If the last Td vaccination was received <10 years ago, Tdap should be administered during the immediate postpartum period. A dose of Tdap is recommended for postpartum women, close contacts of infants aged <12 months, and all healthcare personnel with direct patient contact if they have not previously received Tdap. An interval as short as two years from the last Td vaccination is suggested, though shorter intervals may be used. Td may be deferred during pregnancy, with Tdap substituted in the immediate postpartum period, or Tdap may be administered instead of Td during pregnancy. For wound management, consult ACIP recommendations regarding the use of Td. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination HPV vaccination is recommended at ages 11 or 12, with catch-up vaccination for individuals aged 13–26 years. However, sexually active females should still be vaccinated according to age-based recommendations. Females who have not been infected with any of the HPV types covered by the vaccine (types 6, 11, 16, and 18 for HPV4; types 16 and 18 for HPV2) derive the full benefit of vaccination. Vaccination is less effective for females already infected with one or more of the HPV types included in the vaccine. HPV4 or HPV2 may be administered to individuals with a history of genital warts, abnormal Papanicolaou (Pap) test results, or a positive HPV DNA test, as these conditions do not indicate prior infection with all vaccine HPV types. HPV4 may also be administered to males aged 9–26 years to reduce the risk of acquiring genital warts. A complete series of either HPV4 or HPV2 consists of three doses: the second dose should be given 1–2 months after the first, and the third dose should be given six months after the first. Although HPV vaccination is not specifically recommended for individuals with certain medical conditions, it may still be administered to these individuals because the vaccine is not a live-virus vaccine. However, the immune response and vaccine efficacy may be lower in individuals with these medical conditions compared to those who are immunocompetent. Varicella Vaccination All adults without evidence of immunity to varicella should receive two doses of the single-antigen varicella vaccine if they have not been previously vaccinated or should receive a second dose if they have only received one dose, unless contraindicated. Special consideration should be given to individuals who have close contact with persons at high risk for severe disease (e.g.g., teachers, childcare employees, residents and staff of institutional settings, college students, military personnel, adults living with children, nonpregnant women of childbearing age, and international travelers). Evidence of immunity to varicella in adults includes: documentation of two doses of varicella vaccine at least four weeks apart; U.S. birth before 1980 (except for healthcare personnel and pregnant women, for whom birth before 1980 is not considered evidence of immunity); a history of varicella or herpes zoster confirmed by a healthcare provider; or laboratory evidence of immunity or disease confirmation. Pregnant women should be assessed for varicella immunity. Women without evidence of immunity should receive the first dose of the varicella vaccine after pregnancy and before discharge from the healthcare facility, with the second dose administered 4–8 weeks later. Herpes Zoster Vaccination A single dose of the zoster vaccine is recommended for adults aged ≥60 years, regardless of whether they have had a prior episode of herpes zoster. Individuals with chronic medical conditions may be vaccinated unless their condition is a contraindication. Measles, Mumps, Rubella (MMR) Vaccination Adults born before 1957 are generally considered immune to measles and mumps. Adults born during or after 1957 should receive at least one dose of the MMR vaccine unless they have a medical contraindication, documentation of vaccination, laboratory evidence of immunity, or physician-diagnosed measles or mumps. A second dose of MMR vaccine is recommended for certain high-risk groups, including those exposed to measles, those in outbreak settings, students in postsecondary institutions, healthcare workers, and international travelers. For mumps, a second dose is recommended for individuals in outbreak settings, students in postsecondary institutions, healthcare workers, and international travelers. Healthcare personnel born before 1957 who lack evidence of immunity should consider receiving two doses of MMR vaccine for measles and mumps and one dose for rubella, especially during outbreaks. Hepatitis A and B Vaccination Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended for individuals at risk, including those in close contact with international adoptees from endemic regions. Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for individuals with behavioral, occupational, or medical risk factors, as well as those in high-risk settings. A three-dose series is standard, with specific schedules for combined hepatitis A and B vaccines or for immunocompromised individuals. Meningococcal Vaccination Meningococcal vaccination is recommended for individuals with medical conditions such as asplenia or complement deficiencies, as well as for first-year college students in dormitories, microbiologists exposed to Neisseria meningitidis, military recruits, and travelers to endemic regions.
